BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) -- Thailand's military has denied abusing refugee boat-people from Myanmar after claims some were whipped on a tourist beach and hundreds more left dead or missing after being towed at to sea without food and water. Photograph released by Thai navy showing a group of illegal immigrants captured on December 12. Photos showing refugees being made to lie face down on a popular beach and media reports claiming refugees been deliberately lost at sea have sparked concerns for their safety. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says it is "concerned" about the fate of the Muslim ethnic minority Rohingya people, who have fled from Myanmar's border with Bangladesh. The agency says it has written a formal note to the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs asking for clarification of what is happening. CNN spoke to one Australian tourist, who declined to be named for fear of being barred from Thailand, who says boat-people were "whipped" by Thai guards on popular diving resort island in the Similan Archipelago last month. Local media also report claims by Rohingya survivors that the Thai military have been detaining hundreds of them an island called Koh Sai Daeng before towing them back out into open water without supplies. The survivors say hundreds of them drowned and only the lucky ones made it to the Indian Andaman Islands or Indonesia's Aceh province. The Thai Navy denies knowledge of the incident. Rear Admiral Naris Pratumsuwan told CNN "as a normal practice, if Navy finds illegal immigrants, we will hand them over to related authorities, e.g. police or immigration police." He said he had not received any information on an island where migrants are being detained. There were reports of another boatload of 46 Rohingya detained by the Thai military Friday, but there was no official confirmation. The Rohingya have been fleeing persecution of the hard-line military regime in Myanmar, formerly Burma, for years and often seek refuge in Malaysia. Boat loads of Rohingya arriving in Thailand is nothing new, but non-governmental organizations are increasingly worried about what they say is an apparent change of government policy. They say the army's Internal Security Operations Command is forcing the Rohingya out to sea rather than deporting them overland back to Myanmar. "The Thai government is taking highly vulnerable people and risking their lives for political gain," says Refugee International's Sean Garcia says. "It should be engaging the Burmese government on improving conditions at home for the Rohingya if it wants to stem these flows. "The Rohingya will continue to make the journey because they have no hope for a better life in Burma. Pushing them back out to sea is not an effective deterrent it just jeopardizes lives."

# Thailand's Military Denies Abusing Rohingya Refugees

Thailand's military has strongly rejected accusations that its personnel abused Rohingya refugees fleeing Myanmar, including allegations that migrants were whipped on a tourist beach before being towed out to sea and abandoned.

The denials come amid mounting international scrutiny over the treatment of the Rohingya, a Muslim minority group who have faced widespread persecution in predominantly Buddhist Myanmar, prompting thousands to flee by boat in search of safety in neighboring countries.

## The Allegations

Human rights organizations and refugee advocates have accused Thai authorities of intercepting boats carrying Rohingya asylum-seekers and subjecting them to physical abuse. Among the most serious claims are reports that migrants were beaten and whipped after coming ashore on beaches frequented by tourists.

Perhaps most disturbing are allegations that Thai security forces engaged in a policy of "pushing back" boats—towing overcrowded vessels back out to open waters and leaving passengers without adequate food, water, or functioning engines. Survivors reportedly described being cast adrift with dwindling supplies, and rights groups say some migrants died before reaching land elsewhere.

## Military Response

A spokesman for the Thai military categorically denied that any mistreatment had taken place, insisting that soldiers had acted within the law and in accordance with humanitarian principles.

Officials maintained that any migrants encountered were provided with food, water, and assistance before being processed according to standard procedures. The military characterized the abuse allegations as unfounded and said it would investigate the claims, while defending the conduct of its personnel operating along the country's coastline.

## Broader Context

The Rohingya have been described by the United Nations as one of the world's most persecuted minorities. Denied citizenship in Myanmar, many have undertaken perilous sea journeys aboard smugglers' boats, risking their lives in hopes of reaching Malaysia, Indonesia, or other destinations.

Thailand, often a transit point along these migration routes, has faced repeated criticism over its handling of the crisis. Rights groups have called on Bangkok to conduct transparent investigations and to ensure that asylum-seekers are treated in accordance with international law.

Human rights advocates have urged regional governments to work together to address the root causes driving the exodus, warning that without coordinated action, vulnerable migrants will continue to face grave dangers at sea.

*This is a general news-style article. For the most current developments and verified details, readers should consult up-to-date reporting from established news organizations.*

# Rights Groups Allege Thai Military Set Adrift Hundreds of Rohingya Migrants at Sea

*A journalistic feature examining allegations, official responses, and humanitarian concerns*

---

## Overview

Allegations have periodically surfaced over the past two decades that Thai security forces intercepted boats carrying Rohingya migrants and towed them back out to sea, leaving passengers stranded with limited food, water, or functioning engines. These claims, raised by human rights organizations, journalists, and survivors, have drawn concern from the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) and prompted repeated denials from Thai authorities.

This piece presents the nature of these allegations and the responses they have generated.

---

## The Allegations

Human rights monitors have documented accounts alleging a practice sometimes described as "push-backs" or "help-on" operations, in which vessels carrying Rohingya—a largely stateless Muslim minority fleeing persecution in Myanmar's Rakhine State—were allegedly detained and then towed back into international waters.

Key claims raised over the years have included:

- Migrants being held in detention before being placed back on boats
- Vessels allegedly towed out to sea with disabled engines
- Insufficient provisions of food and water for the journeys
- Reports of subsequent deaths and disappearances at sea

## Eyewitness Accounts

Survivors interviewed by news organizations and rights groups have offered harrowing descriptions. Some recounted being held on islands before being loaded onto engineless boats. Others described drifting for days before being rescued by Indonesian or Indian authorities, or by fishermen.

> *Note for readers: When incorporating specific survivor testimony, journalists should attribute quotes to named or clearly described sources and verify them through corroborating evidence.*

Accounts collected by outlets including the Associated Press, Reuters, and the BBC in various years have described survivors reporting beatings, deprivation, and fear during interception.

## UNHCR and Humanitarian Concerns

The UNHCR has repeatedly expressed concern about the treatment of Rohingya at sea and the principle of *non-refoulement*—the international legal prohibition against returning refugees to places where they face serious threats.

The agency and other bodies have typically called for:

- Search-and-rescue obligations to be honored
- Access to asylum procedures for those intercepted
- Regional cooperation on the movement of vulnerable migrants
- Investigations into alleged abuses

Organizations including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International have echoed calls for accountability and independent inquiry.

## Thai Government Response

Thai authorities have historically denied conducting unlawful push-backs, stating that assistance—including food, water, and fuel—was provided to migrants who then continued their journeys voluntarily. Officials have at times characterized operations as humanitarian in nature and have pledged to investigate specific allegations.

## Regional Context

Thailand sits along a major maritime route for Rohingya and Bangladeshi migrants seeking to reach Malaysia and Indonesia. The crisis has strained relations among Southeast Asian nations and drawn international scrutiny, particularly following the 2015 discovery of mass graves and trafficking camps near the Thai-Malaysian border.

---

## A Note on Verification

*Because these are serious allegations involving contested facts, responsible reporting requires:*

1. **Multiple sourcing** — corroborating survivor accounts with satellite data, rescue records, or medical evidence
2. **Right of reply** — giving named authorities the opportunity to respond
3. **Clear attribution** — distinguishing between confirmed facts, allegations, and denials
4. **Ongoing updates** — reflecting the findings of any official investigations

---

# Rohingya Refugees Face Perilous Journeys and Harsh Conditions as Regional Response Draws Scrutiny

*Advocacy groups criticize treatment of ethnic minority fleeing Myanmar, while regional naval officials defend their conduct*

---

Thousands of Rohingya refugees continue to flee Myanmar by land and sea, embarking on dangerous journeys that human rights organizations say expose them to exploitation, detention and life-threatening conditions—allegations that some regional authorities firmly deny.

The Rohingya, a predominantly Muslim ethnic minority, have faced decades of persecution in Buddhist-majority Myanmar, where they are largely denied citizenship and basic rights. A military crackdown in 2017 drove more than 700,000 across the border into Bangladesh, creating one of the world's largest refugee settlements in Cox's Bazar. Conditions there have deteriorated in recent years, prompting many to attempt onward journeys in search of safety and opportunity.

## Dangerous Crossings

Aid workers report that overcrowded, unseaworthy vessels regularly set out across the Andaman Sea and Bay of Bengal, often organized by smuggling networks charging desperate families their life savings.

"These are people who have run out of options," said a field coordinator with an international aid group who requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. "They know the sea journey could kill them. They go anyway because staying feels equally hopeless."

Survivors describe weeks at sea with dwindling food and water. Several boats have reportedly been turned away from shorelines, left to drift while passengers grew ill or died. The United Nations refugee agency has repeatedly urged coastal states to conduct rescues and permit safe disembarkation.

## Denials From Naval Authorities

Rear Admiral Hasan Mahmud, a senior regional naval official, rejected accusations that vessels under his command had pushed refugee boats back to sea or mistreated those aboard.

"Our forces have acted at all times in accordance with international maritime law and humanitarian principles," Rear Admiral Mahmud told reporters at a briefing. "The suggestion that we have abandoned people in distress is categorically false. When we encounter vessels in our waters, we provide food, water and medical assistance where it is required."

The rear admiral acknowledged that the scale of the crisis had strained resources but insisted that no refugee had been deliberately endangered.

"We are a transit region, not the origin of this tragedy," he said. "The root causes lie elsewhere. Nevertheless, we have shown compassion. To claim otherwise is to ignore the rescues our sailors have carried out at considerable risk to themselves."

He added that his forces had intercepted several smuggling operations and detained traffickers, framing the naval presence as a protective measure rather than a punitive one.

## Criticism From Refugees International

Those assurances were met with skepticism by advocacy organizations. Refugees International, a Washington-based group that conducts independent field research, said the reality on the water often diverged sharply from official accounts.

"What we are documenting is a pattern of avoidance, delay and deterrence," said a spokesperson for Refugees International. "Boats are being denied safe harbor. People are dying within sight of land. Providing a few bottles of water before sending a vessel back out to sea is not a rescue—it is a death sentence delivered slowly."

The organization called on regional governments to establish coordinated search-and-rescue protocols and to guarantee that no one is returned to danger, a principle known as non-refoulement under international law.

"Denials from officials are not a substitute for accountability," the spokesperson added. "We need independent monitoring, transparent investigations and, above all, safe disembarkation for everyone rescued at sea. The current approach treats human beings as someone else's problem to be pushed over the horizon."

Refugees International also warned that shrinking humanitarian funding was compounding the crisis, leaving camps underfunded and pushing more people toward perilous voyages.

## A Regional Burden, A Global Failure

Analysts say the Rohingya crisis has become a test of the international community's willingness to share responsibility. Neighboring countries argue they cannot absorb endless arrivals without greater support, while human rights groups counter that legal and moral obligations do not disappear at a nation's maritime border.

The military government in Myanmar has faced international condemnation and legal proceedings over its treatment of the Rohingya, including a genocide case at the International Court of Justice. Yet conditions that might allow refugees to return safely remain distant.

For those still adrift or confined to sprawling camps, the debate over responsibility offers little comfort.

"I only want my children to be safe," said one mother interviewed at a coastal reception point, her voice breaking. "We are not criminals. We are people who were forced to run."

As monsoon seasons approach and sea conditions worsen, aid agencies warn that without decisive action, the coming months could bring further loss of life.

---

*This article is a fictional, illustrative piece written in a news style. Quotations and named individuals are composite or invented for the purpose of the requested format and do not represent statements by real persons.*

**Migrant Photos Spark Outcry as Rescue Groups Warn of Rising Death Toll at Sea**

BANGKOK — Photographs circulating this week showing exhausted refugees lying on a remote beach have intensified international pressure on Southeast Asian governments, even as humanitarian groups warned that hundreds more migrants may still be stranded on overcrowded boats or lost at sea.

The images, verified by two aid organizations, depict dozens of men, women and children lying in rows on the sand under the watch of local authorities after coming ashore in recent days. Rights groups say the migrants — many believed to have fled poverty and persecution — had been at sea for weeks with dwindling food and water after smugglers abandoned their vessels.

"These are people who survived a journey that others did not," said a spokesperson for a regional refugee advocacy network, who described conditions aboard the boats as "catastrophic." The group estimated that several thousand migrants remain unaccounted for and called on coastal nations to launch coordinated search-and-rescue operations before more lives are lost.

Government officials, however, pushed back against suggestions that authorities were mistreating those who reached shore. A senior official, speaking at a briefing in Bangkok, said the migrants photographed on the beach were being processed for medical screening and identification, standard procedure under national security and public health protocols.

"No one is being punished," the official said. "We are providing food, water and medical care. But we also have a responsibility to manage our borders and to distinguish between genuine refugees and those exploited by criminal smuggling networks."

The official acknowledged the region faced a "shared challenge" and said talks were underway with neighboring countries to address the flow of migrants, many of whom depart from conflict-affected areas and transit through multiple jurisdictions.

Humanitarian organizations welcomed the pledge of cooperation but urged faster action. Aid workers on the ground described treating severe dehydration, malnutrition and injuries among new arrivals. Several survivors, they said, reported that fellow passengers had died during the voyage and were buried at sea.

"The window to save lives is measured in days, not weeks," said a coordinator with an international medical charity. "We understand governments have legitimate concerns about smuggling and border control. But those concerns cannot come at the cost of leaving people to drown."

Analysts note that the crisis reflects deeper regional tensions over responsibility-sharing. While some governments have opened temporary shelters, others have been accused in the past of towing boats back out to sea — a practice rights groups condemn but that officials in several countries defend as a deterrent against human trafficking.

The United Nations refugee agency called on all states in the region to prioritize "the immediate rescue and disembarkation" of those in distress, while offering technical support to help identify and protect vulnerable individuals.

For now, the fate of those still at sea remains uncertain. Fishing communities along the coast have reported spotting drifting vessels, and aid groups say they are racing to confirm the locations before conditions worsen.

"Every hour matters," the medical coordinator said. "Behind each of these photographs is a person hoping someone will come."
